nodes.name: Classical Bernstein operator $B_n$
nodes.statement: the classical Bernstein operator $B_{n}: C\left[ 0,1\right] \rightarrow \operatorname{Span}\{1, x, \dots, x^n\},$ defined by \begin{equation} B_{n}f\left( x\right) =\sum_{k=0}^{n}f\left( \frac{k}{n}\right) \binom{n}{k} x^{k}\left( 1-x\right) ^{n-k} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The classical Bernstein operator sends $f\in C[0,1]$ to $\sum_k f(k/n)\binom{n}{k}x^k(1-x)^{n-k}$ in the polynomials of degree $\le n$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Berens-DeVore extremal characterization of $B_n$
nodes.statement: They show that for every $n$, $L_n x^2 \ge B_n x^2$, and if for some $t\in (0,1)$, $L_n t^2 = B_n t^2$, then $L_n \equiv B_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Within the Berens-DeVore class, $B_n$ minimizes $L_n x^2$, and equality at a single interior point forces $L_n\equiv B_n$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
assumptions: operators $L_n: C\left[ 0,1\right] \rightarrow \operatorname{Span}\{1, x, \dots, x^n\},$ fixing $1$ and $x$, and such that $(L_nf)^{(j)}\geq 0$ if $f^{(j)}\geq 0$ for $j=0,1,2,\cdots,n$
conclusions: for every $n$, $L_n x^2 \ge B_n x^2$
if for some $t\in (0,1)$, $L_n t^2 = B_n t^2$, then $L_n \equiv B_n$

nodes.name: $L_n$ is strictly worse than $B_n$ on $x^2$
nodes.statement: Since $B_n x^2 \ge x^2$, $L_n$ performs strictly worse than $B_n$ (unless $L_n \equiv B_n$) at least for $x^2$.

nodes.name: Bernstein basis $p_{n,k}$ for polynomials
nodes.statement: Denote by $p_{n,k} (x) := \binom{n}{k} x^{k}\left( 1-x\right) ^{n-k}$ the elements of the Bernstein basis for the space of polynomials.

nodes.name: The class $\mathcal{L}_n$ of positive linear operators
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal L_n$ be the class of positive linear operators $L_n: C\left[ 0,1\right] \rightarrow \operatorname{Span}\{1, x, \dots, x^n\}$ fixing $1$ and $x$ (so $L_n$ preserves affine functions) and defined by \begin{equation} L_n f (x) := \sum_{k=0}^{n} \lambda_{n,k}(f) p_{n, k} (x), \ \ \ \ \mbox{ where } \ \ \ \ \lambda_{n,k}(f) := \int_0^1 f d \mu_{n,k}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal L_n$ is the class of positive linear operators into $\mathrm{Span}\{1,\dots,x^n\}$ that fix $1$ and $x$ and act by integrating $f$ against measures $\mu_{n,k}$ in the Bernstein basis.

nodes.name: $B_n$ dominates convex functions
nodes.statement: Recall that if $\phi$ is convex on $[0,1]$, then $B_n\phi \ge \phi$ on that interval.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results
conclusions: $B_n\phi \ge \phi$ on that interval

nodes.name: Optimality of $B_n$ within $\mathcal{L}_n$ for convex functions
nodes.statement: From \cite[Theorem 1]{BuQue} and the generalization in \cite[Theorem 2]{CC}, it is known that $L_n\phi \ge B_n\phi$ for every convex function $\phi$ and every $L_n \in \mathcal L_n$, and furthermore, $L_n\equiv B_n$ if $L_n\psi (t) = B_n\psi (t)$ for some strictly convex function $\psi$ and some $t\in (0,1)$.
nodes.statement_short: For every convex $\phi$ and every $L_n\in\mathcal L_n$ one has $L_n\phi\ge B_n\phi$, with equality at one point for a strictly convex $\psi$ forcing $L_n\equiv B_n$.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results

assumptions: every convex function $\phi$ and every $L_n \in \mathcal L_n$
conclusions: $L_n\phi \ge B_n\phi$ for every convex function $\phi$ and every $L_n \in \mathcal L_n$
$L_n\equiv B_n$ if $L_n\psi (t) = B_n\psi (t)$ for some strictly convex function $\psi$ and some $t\in (0,1)$

nodes.name: Optimality is non-asymptotic
nodes.statement: In this sense the operator $B_n$ approximates convex functions optimally within the class $\mathcal L_n$. We emphasize that this is not an asymptotic optimality result, where $n$ is required to approach $\infty$. Instead, best approximation holds for each fixed $n$.

nodes.name: Normalization consequences of $L_n1\equiv1$ and $L_nx\equiv x$
nodes.statement: Observe that by uniqueness of the coefficients of the basis functions, the condition $L_n 1 \equiv 1$ entails that each $\mu_{n,k}$ is a probability measure, while $L_n x \equiv x$ entails that the expectation of $x$ with respect to $\mu_{n,k}$ is $\int_0^1 x d \mu_{n,k} (x) = k/n$.
nodes.statement_short: Fixing $1$ makes each $\mu_{n,k}$ a probability measure; fixing $x$ pins its mean at $k/n$.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results
conclusions: each $\mu_{n,k}$ is a probability measure
the expectation of $x$ with respect to $\mu_{n,k}$ is $\int_0^1 x d \mu_{n,k} (x) = k/n$

nodes.name: Dropping $L_nx\equiv x$ breaks convexity preservation
nodes.statement: If the assumption $L_n x \equiv x$ is dropped, then the resulting operator may fail to preserve convexity, and may approximate some convex functions better than $B_n$ (while in other cases the approximation will be worse, notably for $x$ itself).
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results

nodes.name: Generalized Bernstein operator $\mathcal{B}_{n,j}$
nodes.statement: Let $1 < j \le n$. In \cite[Proposition 11]{AKR3} and in \cite[Example 5.3]{Mazu09}, a generalized Bernstein operator $\mathcal{B}_{n,j}$ fixing $1$ and $x^{j}$, is defined by \begin{equation*} \mathcal{B}_{n,j}f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}f\left( \left[ \frac{k(k-1)\cdots (k-j+1)}{ n(n-1)\cdots (n-j+1)}\right] ^{1/j}\right) \binom{n}{k}x^{k}(1-x)^{n-k}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal B_{n,j}$ samples $f$ at the $j$-th-root falling-factorial nodes against the Bernstein basis and fixes $1$ and $x^j$.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results
nodes.origin_citation: Aldaz, Kounchev & Render, Proposition 11; Mazure 2009, Example 5.3

nodes.name: Example 1: the operators $\mathcal{B}_{n,j}$
nodes.statement: Let $1 < j \le n$. In \cite[Proposition 11]{AKR3} and in \cite[Example 5.3]{Mazu09}, a generalized Bernstein operator $\mathcal{B}_{n,j}$ fixing $1$ and $x^{j}$, is defined by \begin{equation*} \mathcal{B}_{n,j}f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}f\left( \left[ \frac{k(k-1)\cdots (k-j+1)}{ n(n-1)\cdots (n-j+1)}\right] ^{1/j}\right) \binom{n}{k}x^{k}(1-x)^{n-k}. \end{equation*} In particular, if $j = 1$ this is the classical Bernstein operator. However, for $j > 1$ and all $k = 1, 2, \dots$, $\mathcal{B}_{n,j} x^k < B_{n} x^k$ on $(0,1)$, since the operator $\mathcal{B}_{n,j}$ samples the strictly increasing functions $x^k$ at nodes lower than those of $B_{n}$ (except the first and the last nodes, which are 0 and 1 in both cases). It is shown in \cite[Example 17]{AKR3} that if $1\le k\le j$, then $\mathcal{B}_{n,j} x^k \le x^k$, while if $j\le k$, then $\mathcal{B}_{n,j} x^k \ge x^k$. Hence, on $(0,1)$, ${B}_{n} x^k > \mathcal{B}_{n,j} x^k \ge x^k$ when $j\le k$. Of course, $\mathcal{B}_{n,j}$ does not preserve convexity, since $$ \mathcal{B}_{n,j} (1 - x) = \mathcal{B}_{n,j}(1) -\mathcal{B}_{n,j}( x) > 1- B_n (x) = 1 - x $$ whenever $x\in (0,1)$. But $\mathcal{B}_{n,j}$ does preserve $(1,x^j)$-convexity, defined below.
nodes.statement_short: For $j>1$ the operator $\mathcal B_{n,j}$ undershoots $B_n$ on every $x^k$, fails to preserve ordinary convexity, but preserves $(1,x^j)$-convexity.

nodes.statement: It is shown in \cite[Example 17]{AKR3} that if $1\le k\le j$, then $\mathcal{B}_{n,j} x^k \le x^k$, while if $j\le k$, then $\mathcal{B}_{n,j} x^k \ge x^k$.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results
conclusions: $\mathcal{B}_{n,j} x^k \le x^k$
$\mathcal{B}_{n,j} x^k \ge x^k$

nodes.name: Extended Chebyshev space
nodes.statement: An \emph{extended Chebyshev space} $U_{n}$ of dimension $n+1$ over the interval $\left[ a,b\right] $ is an $n+1$ dimensional subspace of $C^{n}\left( \left[a,b\right] \right)$ such that each function $f\in U_{n}$ not vanishing identically, has at most $n$ zeros in $\left[ a,b\right]$, counting multiplicities.
nodes.statement_short: An extended Chebyshev space of dimension $n+1$ on $[a,b]$ is a subspace of $C^n([a,b])$ in which no nonzero function has more than $n$ zeros counted with multiplicity.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results
differentia: each function $f\in U_{n}$ not vanishing identically, has at most $n$ zeros in $\left[ a,b\right]$, counting multiplicities

nodes.name: Non-negative Bernstein basis
nodes.statement: It is well-known that extended Chebyshev spaces possess \emph{non-negative Bernstein bases}, i.e. collections of non-negative functions $p_{n,k},k=0,...,n,$ in $U_{n}$, such that each $p_{n,k}$ has a zero of order $k$ at $a$ and a zero of order $n-k$ at $b$, for $k=0,...,n$.
nodes.statement_short: A non-negative Bernstein basis of $U_n$ is a family of non-negative $p_{n,k}$ with a zero of order $k$ at $a$ and order $n-k$ at $b$; extended Chebyshev spaces always have one.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results
differentia: each $p_{n,k}$ has a zero of order $k$ at $a$ and a zero of order $n-k$ at $b$, for $k=0,...,n$

nodes.name: Generalized Bernstein operator $\mathcal{B}_n$
nodes.statement: Now let us select two functions $f_{0},f_{1}\in U_{n},$ such that $f_{0} >0 $ and $f_{1}/f_{0}$ is strictly increasing (these functions play the role of 1 and $x$ in the classical case). It is sometimes possible to define a generalized Bernstein operator $\mathcal{B}_{n}:C\left[ a,b\right] \rightarrow U_{n}$ fixing $f_{0}$ and $f_{1}$, by first suitably choosing nodes $t_{n,0},...,t_{n,n}\in \left[ a,b\right]$ such that $t_{n,0} = a$ and $t_{n,n}= b$, second, by selecting appropriate weights $\alpha _{n,0},...,\alpha _{n,n} > 0$, and finally, by setting \begin{equation} \mathcal{B}_{n}\left( f\right) =\sum_{k=0}^{n}f\left( t_{n,k}\right) \alpha _{n,k}p_{n,k}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Given $f_0>0$ and $f_1/f_0$ strictly increasing in $U_n$, a generalized Bernstein operator fixes $f_0,f_1$ via nodes $t_{n,k}$ with $t_{n,0}=a$, $t_{n,n}=b$ and positive weights $\alpha_{n,k}$.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results
differentia: nodes $t_{n,0},...,t_{n,n}\in \left[ a,b\right]$ such that $t_{n,0} = a$ and $t_{n,n}= b$

nodes.name: Existence of $\mathcal{B}_n$ is assumed
nodes.statement: In this section, we shall {\em assume} that $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ exists (fixing the given functions)
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results

nodes.name: Generalized Bernstein operator with weights absorbed
nodes.statement: For simplicity in the notation, we relabel the basis functions so that they already incorporate the weights $\alpha _{n,k}$. Thus, (\ref{eqBern}) becomes \begin{equation} \mathcal{B}_{n}\left( f\right) =\sum_{k=0}^{n}f\left( t_{n,k}\right) p_{n,k}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results

nodes.name: Standing conditions on $f_0$ and $f_1$
nodes.statement: The functions $f_{0}$ and $f_{1}$ are always assumed to satisfy the conditions ``$f_{0} >0$" and ``$f_{1}/f_{0}$ is strictly increasing".
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results

nodes.name: Existence and non-existence of $\mathcal{B}_n$ for given $f_0,f_1$
nodes.statement: Given an extended Chebyshev space $U_n$, it is always possible to {\em select} some pair $f_0$ and $f_1$ in $U_n$ for which a generalized Bernstein operator can be defined (cf. \cite[Corollary 8]{AKR3}). However, for some choices of $f_0$ and $f_1$, $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ may fail to exist. For instance, it is well known that if $0 < b < 2\pi$, then $U_3 :=\operatorname{Span} \{1,x, \cos x, \sin x\}$ on the interval $[0,b]$ is an extended Chebyshev space. But there is no generalized Bernstein operator $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ fixing $1$ and $x$ if $b=5$ (for instance) while such $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ does exist if $b = 4$, cf. \cite[Theorem 25]{AKR3}.
nodes.statement_short: Some admissible pair $f_0,f_1$ always exists, but for particular choices (e.g. $1,x$ in $\mathrm{Span}\{1,x,\cos x,\sin x\}$ on $[0,5]$) no $\mathcal B_n$ exists.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results
nodes.origin_citation: Aldaz, Kounchev & Render, Corollary 8 and Theorem 25

nodes.name: Endpoint interpolation of $\mathcal{B}_n$
nodes.statement: The condition on the zeros of $p_{n,k}$ entails that, like the classical Bernstein operator, the operators given by (\ref{eqBern}) interpolate functions at the endpoints of the interval $[a,b]$: Since $f_0$ is strictly positive, from $f_0 (a) = \mathcal{B}_{n}\left( f_0\right) (a) = f_0\left( a\right) \alpha _{n, 0}p_{n,0} (a)$ we conclude that $\alpha _{n, 0}p_{n,0} (a) = 1$. Likewise, $\alpha_{n, n}p_{n,n} (b) = 1$, so we always have $\mathcal{B}_{n}\left( f\right) (a) = f(a)$ and $\mathcal{B}_{n}\left( f\right) (b) = f(b)$.
nodes.statement_short: The zero orders of $p_{n,k}$ force $\alpha_{n,0}p_{n,0}(a)=\alpha_{n,n}p_{n,n}(b)=1$, so $\mathcal B_n f$ interpolates $f$ at both endpoints.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results

nodes.name: $(f_0,f_1)$-convexity
nodes.statement: Convexity of $\phi$ can be defined by saying that if we interpolate between $\phi (x)$ and $\phi(y)$ using an affine function $h$, then on $[x,y]$ the graph of $\phi$ lies below the graph of $h$. If instead of affine functions we use $(f_0, f_1)$-affine functions, that is, functions in $\operatorname{Span} \{f_0, f_1\}$, we obtain the corresponding notion of {\em $(f_0, f_1)$-convexity}. Thus, ordinary convexity corresponds to $(1,x)$-convexity.
nodes.statement_short: $(f_0,f_1)$-convexity replaces affine interpolants by elements of $\mathrm{Span}\{f_0,f_1\}$; $(1,x)$-convexity is ordinary convexity.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results
differentia: instead of affine functions we use $(f_0, f_1)$-affine functions, that is, functions in $\operatorname{Span} \{f_0, f_1\}$

nodes.name: Strict $(f_0,f_1)$-convexity
nodes.statement: Strict $(f_0, f_1)$-convexity is defined analogously to strict convexity.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results

nodes.name: $\mathcal{B}_n$ preserves $(f_0,f_1)$-convexity
nodes.statement: It is shown in \cite[Theorem 22]{AKR3} (cf. also \cite[Proposition 4.14]{Mazu09}) that a generalized Bernstein operator $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ fixing $f_0$ and $f_1$ preserves $(f_0, f_1)$-convexity.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results
nodes.origin_citation: Aldaz, Kounchev & Render, Theorem 22; Mazure 2009, Proposition 4.14
assumptions: a generalized Bernstein operator $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ fixing $f_0$ and $f_1$
conclusions: preserves $(f_0, f_1)$-convexity

nodes.name: $\mathcal{B}_n$ generally fails to preserve standard convexity
nodes.statement: We would like to stress the point that $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ will in general {\em fail} to preserve standard convexity (recall example \ref{ex1}). It will be shown in Section 3 that likewise, the standard Bernstein operator ${B}_{n}$ does not in general preserve strengthened forms of convexity, such as $(1,e^x)$-convexity for increasing functions.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results

nodes.name: Bessenyei-Pales characterization of $(f_0,f_1)$-convexity
nodes.statement: Let $I:= (f_1/f_0)([a,b])$. Then $\phi\in C[a,b]$ is $(f_0, f_1)$-convex if and only if $(\phi/f_0) \circ (f_1/f_0)^{-1} \in C\left(I\right)$ is convex in the standard sense.
nodes.statement_short: $\phi$ is $(f_0,f_1)$-convex exactly when $(\phi/f_0)\circ(f_1/f_0)^{-1}$ is convex in the usual sense on $I=(f_1/f_0)([a,b])$.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results
conclusions: $\phi\in C[a,b]$ is $(f_0, f_1)$-convex if and only if $(\phi/f_0) \circ (f_1/f_0)^{-1} \in C\left(I\right)$ is convex in the standard sense

nodes.name: Change of variables between convexity and $(1,f_1)$-convexity
nodes.statement: In particular, if $f_0 = 1$, the relationship between convexity and $(1, f_1)$-convexity is given by a simple change of variables (determined by $f_1$). For instance, returning to Example \ref{ex1}, and to the functions considered there, we see that if $1 \le k \le j$, then $x^k$ is $(1, x^j)$-concave, while if $j \le k \le n$, then $x^k$ is $(1, x^j)$-convex.
nodes.statement_short: When $f_0=1$ the two notions differ by the change of variables $f_1$; e.g. $x^k$ is $(1,x^j)$-concave for $k\le j$ and $(1,x^j)$-convex for $k\ge j$.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results
conclusions: the relationship between convexity and $(1, f_1)$-convexity is given by a simple change of variables (determined by $f_1$)
if $1 \le k \le j$, then $x^k$ is $(1, x^j)$-concave, while if $j \le k \le n$, then $x^k$ is $(1, x^j)$-convex

nodes.name: Proof of the strict-convexity lemma is omitted
nodes.statement: Before we prove the announced optimality property of generalized Bernstein operators, we need the following lemma. It is entirely analogous to Theorem \ref{bepa}, save that strict convexity replaces convexity throughout. The proof is also essentially the same, and thus we omit it. Basically, all one needs to do is to use strict inequalities $>$ instead of $\ge$, at the appropriate places.

nodes.name: Strict $(f_0,f_1)$-convexity characterization
nodes.statement: Let $I:= (f_1/f_0)([a,b])$. Then $\psi\in C[a,b]$ is strictly $(f_0, f_1)$-convex if and only if $(\psi/f_0) \circ (f_1/f_0)^{-1} \in C\left(I\right)$ is strictly convex.
nodes.statement_short: The strict analogue of the Bessenyei-Pales criterion: $\psi$ is strictly $(f_0,f_1)$-convex iff $(\psi/f_0)\circ(f_1/f_0)^{-1}$ is strictly convex.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions and Optimality Results
conclusions: $\psi\in C[a,b]$ is strictly $(f_0, f_1)$-convex if and only if $(\psi/f_0) \circ (f_1/f_0)^{-1} \in C\left(I\right)$ is strictly convex

nodes.name: Optimality of the generalized Bernstein operator
nodes.statement: Let $U_{n}\subset C^{n}\left[ a,b\right]$ be an extended Chebyshev space containing the functions $f_0$ and $f_1$, with $f_0 > 0$ and $f_1/f_0$ strictly increasing. Suppose there exists a generalized Bernstein operator $\mathcal{B}_{n}:C\left[ a,b\right] \rightarrow U_{n}$ fixing $f_{0}$ and $f_{1}$. Let the operator $L_{n}:C\left[ a,b\right] \rightarrow U_{n}$, subject to $L_n f_0 = f_0$ and $L_n f_1 = f_1$, be defined by \begin{equation} L_{n}\left( f\right) =\sum_{k=0}^{n}\lambda_{n,k} (f) p_{n,k}, \end{equation} where $p_{n,k}$ has the same meaning as in (\ref{eqber}), and $\lambda_{n,k}(f) $ is obtained from $f$ and the positive measure $\mu_{n,k}$ via \begin{equation} \lambda_{n, k}(f) := f_0 (t_{n,k}) \int_a^b f d \mu_{n,k}. \end{equation} Then, for every $(f_0, f_1)$-convex function $\phi$, we have $\phi\le \mathcal{B}_{n} \phi \le L_n \phi$. Moreover, if for some $t\in (a,b)$ and some strictly $(f_0, f_1)$-convex function $\psi$ we have $\mathcal{B}_{n} \psi (t) = L_n \psi (t)$, then $\mathcal{B}_{n} \equiv L_n$.

nodes.name: Chains of extended Chebyshev spaces with converging operators
nodes.statement: There are known examples of chains of extended Chebyshev spaces, for which their associated generalized Bernstein operators exist and converge strongly to the identity. An instance is given by the operators $\mathcal{B}_{n,j}$ described in Example \ref{ex1} (cf. \cite[Proposition 11]{AKR3} or \cite[Theorem 6.1]{Mazu09} for the convergence assertion). As was observed in Example \ref{ex1}, the operators $\mathcal{B}_{n,j}$ preserve $(1,x^j)$-convexity, and fail to preserve ordinary convexity when $j > 1$.

nodes.origin_citation: Aldaz, Kounchev & Render, Proposition 11; Mazure 2009, Theorem 6.1

nodes.name: Degeneracy of $\mathcal{B}_{n,j}$ and the plan for this section
nodes.statement: Nevertheless, these operators are somewhat degenerate in that the sequences of nodes are not strictly increasing, due to the fact that for $j>1$, $f_1(x) = x^j$ has a zero of order at least two at zero, and in particular, $f^\prime_1(0) = 0$. Thus, $f^\prime_1$ is not strictly positive on $[0,1]$. We shall use the generalized Bernstein operators introduced by Morigi and Neamtu in \cite{MoNe00} to present a sequence of operators that i) converges to the identity, ii) the operators preserve $(1, e^x)$-convexity, iii) they do not preserve ordinary convexity, iv) they are defined via strictly increasing sequences of nodes (in fact, the nodes are equidistributed), and v) they fix $f_0 = 1$ and $f_1(x)/f_0(x) = f_1(x) = e^x$. Obviously we have $f_1^\prime > 0$ everywhere.
nodes.statement_short: Because $f_1=x^j$ has a double zero at $0$ the nodes of $\mathcal B_{n,j}$ are not strictly increasing, so the Morigi-Neamtu operators with $f_1=e^x$ are used instead.

nodes.name: The functions $\varphi_n$ and $\psi_n$
nodes.statement: Define \begin{equation} \varphi_{n}\left( x\right) :=\frac{e^{\omega_{n}\left( x-b\right) }-e^{\omega_{n}\left( a-b\right) }}{1-e^{\omega_{n}\left( a-b\right) } }\text{ and }\psi_{n}\left( x\right) := 1 - \varphi_{n}\left( x\right) = \frac{1-e^{\omega_{n}\left( x-b\right) }}{1-e^{\omega_{n}\left( a-b\right) }}. \end{equation}

nodes.statement: Recall from (\ref{exponen}) that $\mu_0 = \lambda_0$ and $\mu_1 = \lambda_n$. Using (\ref{bopmone}), (\ref{basisMN}), and (\ref{eqphin}), we obtain \[ \mathcal{B}_{n}\left( e^{\lambda_{0}x}\right) = e^{\lambda_{0}x} \sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}\left( \varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{k}\left( 1-\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{n-k} =e^{\lambda_{0}x} \left(\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) + 1-\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{n} =e^{\lambda_{0}x}. \] Furthermore, \begin{align*} \mathcal{B}_{n}\left( e^{\lambda_{n}x}\right) & = \sum_{k=0}^{n} e^{\lambda_{n}a}e^{\left( \lambda_{n}-\lambda_{0}\right) \frac{k}{n}\left( b-a\right) }e^{\lambda_{0}\left( x-a\right) } \binom{n}{k}\left( \varphi _{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{k}\left( 1-\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{n-k}\\ & = e^{\lambda_{n}a}e^{\lambda_{0}\left( x-a\right) }\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom {n}{k}\left( e^{\omega_{n}\left( b-a\right) }\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{k}\left( 1-\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{n-k}\\ & = e^{\lambda_{n}a}e^{\lambda_{0}\left( x-a\right) }\left( e^{\omega _{n}\left( b-a\right) }\varphi_{n} \left( x\right) + 1-\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{n}\\ & = e^{\lambda_{n}a}e^{\lambda_{0}\left( x-a\right) }\left( \left( e^{\omega_{n}\left( b-a\right) }-1\right) \varphi_{n}\left( x\right) +1\right) ^{n}. \end{align*} But now (\ref{eqphin}) implies that \begin{align*} \left( e^{\omega_{n}\left( b-a\right) }-1\right) \varphi_{n} \left( x\right) +1 & =e^{\omega_{n}\left( b-a\right) }\left( 1-e^{\omega\left( a-b\right) }\right) \varphi_{n} \left( x\right) +1\\ & =e^{\omega_{n}\left( b-a\right) }\left( e^{\omega_{n}\left( x-b\right) }-e^{\omega_{n}\left( a-b\right) }\right) +1=e^{\omega_{n}\left( x-a\right) }, \end{align*} so from the preceding equalities we obtain \[ \mathcal{B}_{n}\left( e^{\lambda_{n}x}\right) =e^{\lambda_{n}a}e^{\lambda_{0}\left( x-a\right) }e^{n\omega_{n}\left( x-a\right) }=e^{\lambda_{n}x}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation: the binomial theorem collapses the sum for $e^{\lambda_0x}$, and after rescaling $\varphi_n$ it collapses again for $e^{\lambda_nx}$.

nodes.name: Binomial collapse for $e^{\lambda_0x}$
nodes.statement: Recall from (\ref{exponen}) that $\mu_0 = \lambda_0$ and $\mu_1 = \lambda_n$. Using (\ref{bopmone}), (\ref{basisMN}), and (\ref{eqphin}), we obtain \[ \mathcal{B}_{n}\left( e^{\lambda_{0}x}\right) = e^{\lambda_{0}x} \sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}\left( \varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{k}\left( 1-\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{n-k} =e^{\lambda_{0}x} \left(\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) + 1-\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{n} =e^{\lambda_{0}x}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the basis into $\mathcal B_n(e^{\lambda_0x})$; the binomial theorem gives $(\varphi_n+1-\varphi_n)^n=1$.

nodes.name: Expand $\mathcal{B}_n(e^{\lambda_nx})$ as a rescaled binomial sum
nodes.statement: Furthermore, \begin{align*} \mathcal{B}_{n}\left( e^{\lambda_{n}x}\right) & = \sum_{k=0}^{n} e^{\lambda_{n}a}e^{\left( \lambda_{n}-\lambda_{0}\right) \frac{k}{n}\left( b-a\right) }e^{\lambda_{0}\left( x-a\right) } \binom{n}{k}\left( \varphi _{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{k}\left( 1-\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{n-k}\\ & = e^{\lambda_{n}a}e^{\lambda_{0}\left( x-a\right) }\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom {n}{k}\left( e^{\omega_{n}\left( b-a\right) }\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{k}\left( 1-\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{n-k}\\ & = e^{\lambda_{n}a}e^{\lambda_{0}\left( x-a\right) }\left( e^{\omega _{n}\left( b-a\right) }\varphi_{n} \left( x\right) + 1-\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{n}\\ & = e^{\lambda_{n}a}e^{\lambda_{0}\left( x-a\right) }\left( \left( e^{\omega_{n}\left( b-a\right) }-1\right) \varphi_{n}\left( x\right) +1\right) ^{n}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the sum with $e^{\omega_n(b-a)}\varphi_n$ and collapse it to $\left((e^{\omega_n(b-a)}-1)\varphi_n+1\right)^n$.

nodes.name: Simplify the bracket using the formula for $\varphi_n$
nodes.statement: But now (\ref{eqphin}) implies that \begin{align*} \left( e^{\omega_{n}\left( b-a\right) }-1\right) \varphi_{n} \left( x\right) +1 & =e^{\omega_{n}\left( b-a\right) }\left( 1-e^{\omega\left( a-b\right) }\right) \varphi_{n} \left( x\right) +1\\ & =e^{\omega_{n}\left( b-a\right) }\left( e^{\omega_{n}\left( x-b\right) }-e^{\omega_{n}\left( a-b\right) }\right) +1=e^{\omega_{n}\left( x-a\right) }, \end{align*}

nodes.name: Morigi-Neamtu operator specialized to $[0,1]$ with $\mu_0=0,\mu_1=1$
nodes.statement: For simplicity, next we take $\left[ a,b\right] $ to be $[0,1]$, $\mu_0 = 0$, and $\mu_1 = 1$. Then the Morigi and Neamtu operator reduces to \begin{equation} \mathcal{B}_{n} f \left( x\right) :=\sum_{k=0}^{n} f\left( \frac{k}{n}\right) \binom {n}{k} \left( \varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{k}\left( 1-\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{n-k}, \end{equation} where by specialization of (\ref{eqphin}) we have \[ \varphi_{n}\left( x\right) =\frac{e^{x/n}-1}{e^{1/n}-1}. \]
nodes.statement_short: On $[0,1]$ with $\mu_0=0,\mu_1=1$ the operator becomes $\sum_k f(k/n)\binom{n}{k}\varphi_n^k(1-\varphi_n)^{n-k}$ with $\varphi_n(x)=(e^{x/n}-1)/(e^{1/n}-1)$.

nodes.name: $\varphi_n$ is convex, increasing and fixes the endpoints
nodes.statement: Observe that since $e^{x/n}$ is convex and increasing, so is $\varphi_{n}$. Furthermore, $\varphi_{n}\left( 0\right) =0$ and $\varphi_{n}\left( 1\right) =1$.

conclusions: since $e^{x/n}$ is convex and increasing, so is $\varphi_{n}$
$\varphi_{n}\left( 0\right) =0$ and $\varphi_{n}\left( 1\right) =1$

nodes.name: Composition identity $\mathcal{B}_nf=B_nf\circ\varphi_n$
nodes.statement: Recalling that $B_n$ denotes the classical Bernstein operator, given by (\ref{defBP}), we see that \begin{equation} \mathcal{B}_{n} f \left( x\right) = B_{n} f \left( \varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The specialized Morigi-Neamtu operator is the classical Bernstein operator precomposed with $\varphi_n$.
nodes.section: 3 On the generalized Bernstein Operator of Morigi and Neamtu

nodes.name: $\mathcal{B}_n$ does not preserve convexity of decreasing convex functions
nodes.statement: From the preceding expression it is immediate that $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ does not in general preserve the convexity of a (decreasing) convex function. Let $h(x) = -x$. Since $B_n h = h$, we have \[ \mathcal{B}_{n} h \left( x\right) =B_{n} h \left( \varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) = - \varphi_{n}\left( x\right). \] But $\varphi_{n}$ is strictly convex, so the image under $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ of the affine (hence convex) function $h$ is the strictly concave function $- \varphi_{n}$.
nodes.statement_short: For $h(x)=-x$ one gets $\mathcal B_nh=-\varphi_n$, which is strictly concave although $h$ is affine.
nodes.section: 3 On the generalized Bernstein Operator of Morigi and Neamtu
conclusions: $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ does not in general preserve the convexity of a (decreasing) convex function

nodes.name: Correction of Mazure, Remark 4.15 (1)
nodes.statement: This shows that the following assertion, contained in \cite[Remark 4.15 (1)]{Mazu09}, is not correct: If $f_0 = 1$, $f_1$ is convex, and $f_1^\prime > 0$ everywhere on $[a,b]$, then the image of a decreasing convex function under $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ is convex (this is claimed to follow from \cite[Proposition 4.14]{Mazu09}, but it does not; we note that Proposition 4.14 from \cite{Mazu09} is correct, cf. \cite[Theorem 22]{AKR3} together with Theorem 4 above for a stronger result).
nodes.statement_short: The counterexample refutes the claim in Mazure's Remark 4.15 (1) that $\mathcal B_n$ maps decreasing convex functions to convex ones, while her Proposition 4.14 remains correct.

nodes.name: Strong convergence of $\mathcal{B}_n$ to the identity
nodes.statement: It is shown in \cite[Theorem 3.3]{MoNe00} that the operators $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ converge strongly to the identity (more general or related results can be found in \cite[Theorem 23]{AKR1} and \cite[Theorem 6.1]{Mazu09}).
nodes.section: 3 On the generalized Bernstein Operator of Morigi and Neamtu
nodes.origin_citation: Morigi & Neamtu 2000, Theorem 3.3; Aldaz, Kounchev & Render, Theorem 23; Mazure 2009, Theorem 6.1
conclusions: the operators $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ converge strongly to the identity

nodes.name: Direct proof of strong convergence in the special case
nodes.statement: Let $g(x) := x$. Since $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ fixes $1$ and $e^x$, by Korovkin's Theorem it suffices to prove that $\mathcal{B}_{n} g$ converges uniformly to $g$ on $[0,1]$. By (\ref{eqnice}), $\mathcal{B}_{n} g = \varphi_{n}$, so it is enough to show that $\varphi_{n}$ converges uniformly to $g$. Since $\varphi_{n}$ is convex and increasing, its derivative achieves its maximum value over $[0,1]$ at $1$. Now let $g_n$ be the affine function with slope $\varphi_{n}^\prime (1)$ passing thorough the point $(1,1)$. By convexity, $g_n \le \varphi_{n} \le g$, so to obtain the uniform convergence it suffices to show that $\lim_{n\to\infty }\varphi_{n}^\prime (1) = 1$. But this follows immediately by writing explicitly $\varphi_{n}^\prime (1)$, and then using L'Hospital rule, or the Taylor expansion for $e^{1/n}$.
nodes.statement_short: By Korovkin's theorem it suffices that $\mathcal B_ng=\varphi_n\to g$ uniformly, which follows from convexity squeezing $\varphi_n$ between an affine minorant and $g$ once $\varphi_n'(1)\to1$.

nodes.name: Reduce to $\mathcal{B}_ng\to g$ by Korovkin's theorem
nodes.statement: Let $g(x) := x$. Since $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ fixes $1$ and $e^x$, by Korovkin's Theorem it suffices to prove that $\mathcal{B}_{n} g$ converges uniformly to $g$ on $[0,1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Since $\mathcal B_n$ fixes $1$ and $e^x$, Korovkin's theorem reduces convergence to the single test function $g(x)=x$.

nodes.statement_short: The composition identity gives $\mathcal B_ng=\varphi_n$, so it suffices that $\varphi_n\to g$ uniformly.

nodes.statement: Since $\varphi_{n}$ is convex and increasing, its derivative achieves its maximum value over $[0,1]$ at $1$. Now let $g_n$ be the affine function with slope $\varphi_{n}^\prime (1)$ passing thorough the point $(1,1)$.

nodes.name: Squeeze $\varphi_n$ and compute $\lim\varphi_n'(1)=1$
nodes.statement: By convexity, $g_n \le \varphi_{n} \le g$, so to obtain the uniform convergence it suffices to show that $\lim_{n\to\infty }\varphi_{n}^\prime (1) = 1$. But this follows immediately by writing explicitly $\varphi_{n}^\prime (1)$, and then using L'Hospital rule, or the Taylor expansion for $e^{1/n}$.

nodes.name: Both failures follow from a general proposition
nodes.statement: We have seen that $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ does not preserve convexity. It is easy to check that $B_n$ does not preserve $(1, e^x)$-convexity either. Actually, both of these facts can be derived from the slightly more general result given next.

nodes.name: Mutual failure of convexity preservation
nodes.statement: Let $f_0 =1$ and $f_1$ be functions in an Extended Chebyshev Space $E$ over the interval $[a,b]$, where $f_1$ is assumed to be strictly increasing and strictly convex. Suppose there exists a generalized Bernstein operator $\mathcal{B}_{n}: C[a,b]\to E$ fixing $f_0$ and $f_1$. Then the classical Bernstein operator ${B}_{n}$ does not preserve $(1, f_1)$-convexity, and the generalized operator $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ does not preserve convexity.
nodes.statement_short: If $f_1$ is strictly increasing and strictly convex and $\mathcal B_n$ fixes $1,f_1$, then $B_n$ fails to preserve $(1,f_1)$-convexity and $\mathcal B_n$ fails to preserve convexity.

nodes.name: Proof of the mutual failure proposition
nodes.statement: For the first assertion, observe that while $f_1$ is trivially $(1, f_1)$-convex, $B_n f_1$ is not. To see why, note that since $B_n f_1 (a) = f_1 (a)$ and $B_n f_1 (b) = f_1 (b)$, the unique function in $\operatorname{Span}\{1, f_1\}$ interpolating $B_n f_1$ at $a$ and $b$ is $f_1$ itself. If $B_n f_1$ were $(1, f_1)$-convex, we would have $B_n f_1 \le f_1$ on $[a,b]$. But $f_1$ is strictly convex, so by Jensen's inequality (including the equality condition) we have $B_n f_1 (x) > f_1(x)$ for all $x\in (a,b)$. An analogous argument yields the second assertion. Set $h(x) = x$, so both $h$ and $-h$ are convex. Towards a contradiction, suppose that $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ preserves convexity. Then $\mathcal{B}_{n} h \le h$ and $\mathcal{B}_{n}(- h) \le -h$, so $\mathcal{B}_{n} h = h$. Fix $x\in (a,b)$, and note that $f\mapsto \mathcal{B}_{n} f(x)$ is a positive linear functional on $C[a,b]$, defined by a probability measure (since $\mathcal{B}_{n} 1 (x) = 1$). Thus we can once more apply Jensen's inequality, in this case to the strictly concave function $f_1^{-1}$, to conclude that $$x = h(x) = \mathcal{B}_{n} h (x) = \mathcal{B}_{n} (f_1^{-1}\circ f_1) (x) > f_1^{-1} \left( \mathcal{B}_{n} f_1 (x)\right) = f_1^{-1}\left( f_1 (x)\right) = x. $$ Alternatively, we can reach the same conclusion without using Jensen's inequality, by observing that if in addition to fixing $1$ and $f_1$, we have $\mathcal{B}_{n} h = h$, then $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ fixes three linearly independent functions, and thus it must be the identity operator (by \cite[Proposition 3.7]{Mazu09}). So again we have a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Jensen's strict inequality gives $B_nf_1>f_1$ on $(a,b)$, contradicting $(1,f_1)$-convexity; the dual argument with $f_1^{-1}$ (or a three-fixed-function count) contradicts convexity preservation.

nodes.name: $B_nf_1$ is not $(1,f_1)$-convex
nodes.statement: For the first assertion, observe that while $f_1$ is trivially $(1, f_1)$-convex, $B_n f_1$ is not. To see why, note that since $B_n f_1 (a) = f_1 (a)$ and $B_n f_1 (b) = f_1 (b)$, the unique function in $\operatorname{Span}\{1, f_1\}$ interpolating $B_n f_1$ at $a$ and $b$ is $f_1$ itself. But $f_1$ is strictly convex, so by Jensen's inequality (including the equality condition) we have $B_n f_1 (x) > f_1(x)$ for all $x\in (a,b)$.
nodes.statement_short: Endpoint interpolation makes $f_1$ the unique $\mathrm{Span}\{1,f_1\}$ interpolant, but Jensen gives $B_nf_1>f_1$ inside.

nodes.name: Alternative argument via three fixed functions
nodes.statement: Alternatively, we can reach the same conclusion without using Jensen's inequality, by observing that if in addition to fixing $1$ and $f_1$, we have $\mathcal{B}_{n} h = h$, then $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ fixes three linearly independent functions, and thus it must be the identity operator (by \cite[Proposition 3.7]{Mazu09}). So again we have a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Alternatively, fixing $1$, $f_1$ and $h$ makes $\mathcal B_n$ the identity, again a contradiction.

nodes.name: Relative strength of $(1,f_1)$-convexity and convexity
nodes.statement: Let $f_1$ be increasing and strictly convex on $[a,b]$. For increasing functions on $[a,b]$, the condition of $(1, f_1)$-convexity is strictly stronger than convexity. Over the decreasing functions on $[a,b]$, convexity is strictly stronger than $(1, f_1)$-convexity.
nodes.statement_short: For increasing functions $(1,f_1)$-convexity is strictly stronger than convexity; for decreasing functions the implication reverses.
nodes.section: 3 On the generalized Bernstein Operator of Morigi and Neamtu
assumptions: Let $f_1$ be increasing and strictly convex on $[a,b]$
conclusions: For increasing functions on $[a,b]$, the condition of $(1, f_1)$-convexity is strictly stronger than convexity
Over the decreasing functions on $[a,b]$, convexity is strictly stronger than $(1, f_1)$-convexity

nodes.name: Proof of the relative strength proposition
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be increasing and $(1, f_1)$-convex on $[a,b]$. Pick $x,y\in [a,b]$ with $x < y$. Since $f(y)\ge f(x)$, the unique interpolant $\psi$ of $f$ at $x$ and $y$ such that $\psi\in\operatorname{Span}\{1, f_1\}$ must be of the form $\psi = c_0 + c_1 f_1$, with $c_1 \ge 0$. Thus $\psi$ is convex, so the unique interpolant $\phi \in\operatorname{Span}\{1, t\}$ of $\psi$ (or $f$) at $x$ and $y$ satisfies $\phi (t) \ge \psi (t) \ge f(t)$ for all $t\in [x,y]$, whence $f$ is convex. Also, $h(t) := t$ is increasing and convex but not $(1, f_1)$-convex, since $h(f^{-1}_1) = f^{-1}_1$ is strictly concave, cf. Lemma \ref{bepas}. The assertion about decreasing functions is proved by the same type of argument, so we omit it.
nodes.statement_short: The $\mathrm{Span}\{1,f_1\}$ interpolant of an increasing $(1,f_1)$-convex $f$ has $c_1\ge0$ hence is convex, forcing $f$ convex; $h(t)=t$ shows strictness.

nodes.name: The interpolant has non-negative $f_1$-coefficient
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be increasing and $(1, f_1)$-convex on $[a,b]$. Pick $x,y\in [a,b]$ with $x < y$. Since $f(y)\ge f(x)$, the unique interpolant $\psi$ of $f$ at $x$ and $y$ such that $\psi\in\operatorname{Span}\{1, f_1\}$ must be of the form $\psi = c_0 + c_1 f_1$, with $c_1 \ge 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity of $f$ forces the unique $\mathrm{Span}\{1,f_1\}$ interpolant $\psi=c_0+c_1f_1$ to have $c_1\ge0$.

nodes.name: Chain the interpolants to conclude $f$ is convex
nodes.statement: Thus $\psi$ is convex, so the unique interpolant $\phi \in\operatorname{Span}\{1, t\}$ of $\psi$ (or $f$) at $x$ and $y$ satisfies $\phi (t) \ge \psi (t) \ge f(t)$ for all $t\in [x,y]$, whence $f$ is convex.
